content: Persistent diarrhoea, defined as diarrhoea lasting more than 14 days, is responsible for approximately one-third of all diarrhoea-related deaths in developing countries according to some studies. Probiotics have been proposed as a potential therapeutic option for managing this condition. The objective of this study was to assess the efficacy of probiotics in treating persistent diarrhoea in children. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and LILACS. Additionally, the authors contacted researchers involved in the included trials, reached out to relevant organizations, and reviewed reference lists. The most recent search was completed on December 13, 2012. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized controlled trials that compared a specific probiotic agent to either a placebo or no probiotic treatment in children suffering from persistent diarrhoea. Two independent reviewers evaluated the eligibility of studies, assessed the risk of bias, and extracted and analyzed the data. Any disagreements were resolved through discussion. Statistical analyses were conducted using a fixed-effect model, and the results for continuous outcomes were expressed as mean differences (MD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Four trials, involving a total of 464 participants, met the inclusion criteria. Among these, one trial was determined to have a low risk of bias. A meta-analysis of two trials (n = 324) demonstrated that probiotics significantly reduced the duration of persistent diarrhoea, with a mean difference of 4.02 days (95% CI: 4.61 to 3.43 days). Additionally, stool frequency was found to decrease in two trials that evaluated this outcome. One trial reported a significant reduction in hospital stay duration, although the sample size was small. Importantly, no adverse events associated with probiotic use were reported in any of the included studies. The authors concluded that there is limited evidence suggesting that probiotics may be effective in treating persistent diarrhoea in children. However, further high-quality research is needed to confirm these findings and establish more definitive recommendations.
